abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for DNA tile self-assembly that transcends traditional Turing-complete computational models. Unlike conventional approaches that simulate sequential computation through tile growth, our model exploits the inherent parallelism of molecular self-assembly to perform massively concurrent information processing. We formalize this new computing paradigm through a hierarchical assembly model incorporating non-deterministic tile placement and energy-guided error correction mechanisms. The computational power analysis reveals that certain decision problems can be solved in O(log n) assembly steps—a complexity unachievable by any deterministic Turing machine with comparable resources. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between our model and λ-calculus, demonstrating that any computable function can be evaluated through controlled self-assembly processes. This work fundamentally redefines the relationship between physical implementation constraints and computational complexity in molecular systems. The proposed paradigm opens unprecedented avenues for solving combinatorial optimization problems through bottom-up molecular fabrication. Our theoretical contributions include novel lower bound proofs for assembly time complexity and a complete characterization of the decision problems tractable within this framework. This research establishes natural computing as a viable alternative paradigm for addressing problems beyond the reach of classical computational theory.

We present a rigorous convergence analysis framework for multi-objective evolutionary algorithms that significantly advances the theoretical understanding of Pareto optimization. While existing analyses rely on asymptotic convergence proofs with weak distributional assumptions, our approach provides non-asymptotic convergence rates under practical conditions. We introduce the concept of ε-Pareto front coverage speed, a quantitative measure that captures how rapidly an algorithm reduces the gap between the current population and the optimal front. By decomposing the dynamics of non-dominated sorting into Markov chain transitions, we prove that the (μ+λ)-EA with appropriate selection pressure achieves O(ε^(-1)·log(μ)) expected iterations to reach ε-Pareto optimality. Our main theoretical contribution is a tight bound on the required population size for maintaining sufficient diversity, demonstrating that previous recommendations underestimate the necessary resources by a factor of O(log n). We further extend the analysis to dynamic environments where objective functions change over time, establishing novel bounds on tracking ability. These results provide actionable guidelines for parameter tuning in evolutionary computation. Our theoretical framework is validated through extensive simulation studies on standard benchmark problems. This work delivers a substantially improved theoretical foundation for multi-objective optimization algorithms with direct implications for practical evolutionary computation implementations.

We introduce a groundbreaking membrane computing architecture that fundamentally reconceptualizes distributed problem-solving through chemically-inspired information processing. Traditional membrane systems operate on symbol-object hierarchies within statically defined membrane structures, limiting their applicability to dynamic real-world scenarios. Our proposed Adaptive Membrane Architecture (AMA) enables dynamic membrane formation, division, and dissolution driven by environmental stimuli and computational requirements. The system comprises three novel components: reactive membranes that alter permeability based on computational state, inter-membrane communication channels modeled after gap junctions in biological systems, and a global environment serving as both communication medium and external memory. We implement a prototype AMA system using programmable microfluidic networks, demonstrating its capability to solve graph coloring problems through emergent self-organization. The execution model exploits maximum parallelism inherent in membrane systems while incorporating feedback mechanisms for hierarchical solution refinement. Our experimental results on NP-complete problems show that AMA achieves solution quality comparable to state-of-the-art algorithms while requiring only O(n) processing elements—a substantial reduction compared to the exponential resources typically demanded. The architecture demonstrates particular strength in handling dynamically changing optimization landscapes, a capability absent in conventional natural computing paradigms. This work establishes membrane computing as a practical framework for scalable, fault-tolerant distributed computing with applications in combinatorial optimization, resource allocation, and autonomous system coordination.

We present an enhanced swarm intelligence optimization system that synergistically integrates particle swarm optimization with neural network-guided exploration for superior performance on complex optimization landscapes. The core innovation lies in embedding a lightweight recurrent neural network within each particle to encode and exploit historical search experience, forming what we term Memory-Augmented Particle Swarm Optimization (MA-PSO). This hybrid approach addresses the fundamental limitation of standard PSO: the inability to retain and utilize long-term search patterns when the swarm reinitializes after convergence. Our system architecture comprises three interconnected modules: a spatial awareness module capturing local neighborhood topology, a temporal memory module maintaining particle-specific exploration history, and a global coordination module enabling information transfer across disconnected subpopulations. The neural memory mechanism employs a gated recurrent unit optimized for the specific dynamics of swarm motion, requiring only 127 parameters per particle to achieve significant performance gains. We evaluate MA-PSO on 30 benchmark functions including CEC competition test suites, demonstrating average improvements of 34.7% in solution quality and 52.3% in convergence speed compared to state-of-the-art PSO variants. The system exhibits particularly strong performance on multi-modal problems requiring exploration of multiple optima and on dynamic optimization scenarios with shifting fitness landscapes. Implementation details for parallel execution on GPU architectures are provided, enabling efficient processing of high-dimensional optimization problems. This work advances swarm intelligence methodology by introducing principled neural memory mechanisms while maintaining the computational simplicity essential to practical deployment.
